data.title: Claude down? Here’s what we know about the outage
data.description:
Anthropic is investigating elevated error rates affecting Claude, Claude Cowork and Claude Code as users report trouble accessing the AI service.

If Claude suddenly stopped working on Tuesday, Sept. 29, you were not necessarily alone. Users attempting to access Anthropic’s popular AI assistant across the web, mobile apps and desktop appeared to be running into authentication and processing problems, leaving some unable to use the service.


The disruption quickly drew attention as reports of problems began climbing. For people who rely on Claude for writing, coding, research and everyday tasks, the outage was a reminder of how quickly a cloud-based AI service can become inaccessible when something goes wrong behind the scenes.


Anthropic has acknowledged that it is investigating elevated error rates affecting several of its services.

Claude users hit unexpected errors

Reports indicated that the problems were not limited to one platform. Users attempting to connect through Claude’s website, iOS and Android apps, as well as the desktop experience, encountered errors while trying to start or continue conversations.

Some users were met with messages indicating that their requests could not be processed. Others appeared to have trouble authenticating their accounts, making it difficult to get into Claude in the first place.

The issue also appeared to affect users with paid subscriptions. That matters because it has become more than a casual chatbot for many customers. Its paid tiers are used by professionals, developers and other users who depend on consistent access to AI tools.

Third-party outage tracking also began showing a noticeable increase in reports, suggesting the problem was broader than isolated account or device issues.

What Anthropic says about the outage

Anthropic’s status page confirmed that the company was investigating elevated error rates across Claude and related products.

The reported disruption included Claude itself, Claude Cowork and Claude Code, indicating that the problem was potentially affecting several parts of Anthropic’s broader AI ecosystem rather than a single interface.

At this stage, the company had not publicly identified a specific root cause or provided a definitive timeline for a full resolution.

That leaves users with an important distinction: an outage can be confirmed without its underlying cause being immediately known. Until Anthropic completes its investigation, it remains unclear whether the disruption stems from infrastructure, authentication, software or another technical issue.

Why the Claude disruption matters

Claude has become a significant player in the rapidly expanding AI assistant market, competing for users who increasingly incorporate generative AI into work and personal routines.

When a service like Claude experiences an outage, the consequences can extend beyond someone being unable to ask a chatbot a question. Developers may lose access to coding tools, workers may be unable to retrieve information from ongoing conversations, and businesses using AI-powered workflows can face interruptions.

For individual users, the experience can be especially frustrating when the service appears to work on one device but fails on another. Authentication errors can also make it difficult to determine whether the problem is with an account or with the platform itself.

What its users can do now

If it is not working, users can check Anthropic’s official status page for updates rather than repeatedly attempting to sign in or reinstall the app.

It may also help to:

  • Check whether the outage is affecting multiple Claude services.
  • Try again later if Anthropic is reporting an active incident.
  • Avoid repeatedly changing account settings while the company investigates.
  • Save important work locally when possible to reduce disruption during future outages.

For now, the most significant development is that Anthropic has acknowledged the service problems and is investigating them. Until the company provides more information, users may have to wait for the affected services to stabilize.

The outage also highlights a growing reality of the AI era: as these tools become woven into everyday work, even a temporary service interruption can quickly become a much bigger inconvenience.

Source: techradar

data.title: Apple’s iOS 27.0.1 update brings 3 essential iPhone fixes
data.description:
iPhone users, it’s time to check your settings.


Apple has released iOS 27.0.1, the first minor update since iOS 27 arrived earlier this month. The new software, which carries the build number 24A446, doesn’t bring any flashy new features. Instead, it focuses on fixing a handful of frustrating bugs that some users have run into since upgrading.


The update is available for every iPhone that supports iOS 27. However, two of its three main fixes are aimed specifically at the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple’s newest and most advanced models.

Here’s a closer look at the three fixes included in the release.

1. Face ID restart fix

The most notable fix addresses a problem with Face ID on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Some owners found that their phones could unexpectedly restart when Face ID failed to recognize them.

Affected users also reported that their devices would sometimes freeze or have trouble when using Face ID inside apps. Because so many people rely on Face ID to unlock their phones, sign in to accounts and approve payments, this bug could be especially disruptive during everyday use.

2. Camera color artifact fix

The second fix involves the camera on a small number of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max devices. In certain lighting conditions, photos taken at 2x zoom with an aperture of f/1.48 could show an unwanted color artifact.

While the issue only affected a limited number of phones, it’s the kind of glitch that can be especially annoying for anyone who bought a Pro model for its camera. The update should help ensure those shots come out looking the way they’re supposed to.

3. Touchscreen responsiveness fix

The third fix has a broader reach. Apple corrected a bug that could cause the touchscreen to stop responding if a user opened Notification Center and Control Center at the same time.

Unlike the first two fixes, this issue wasn’t limited to the newest Pro models. It could affect iPhones running iOS 27 more generally, making this update worth installing even if you don’t own an iPhone 18 Pro.

Updates for other Apple devices

The iPhone isn’t the only device getting attention. Apple also released iPadOS 27.0.1 for iPad and visionOS 27.0.1 for Apple Vision Pro alongside the new iPhone software.

Owners of older devices that can’t run the latest software haven’t been left out either. Apple has also made iOS 26.7.1 and iPadOS 26.7.1 available for those models.

How to install iOS 27.0.1

Getting the update only takes a few taps. Open the Settings app on your iPhone, tap General and then select Software Update. Once iOS 27.0.1 appears, tap Update Now or Download and Install, and enter your passcode if you’re asked for it. Keep your phone connected to power and Wi-Fi while the update installs, since the process can take several minutes and your iPhone will restart when it’s finished.

If you’d rather not check for updates yourself, you can turn on Automatic Updates from the same Software Update screen. With that setting on, your iPhone will download and install new versions of iOS on its own, usually overnight while it’s charging.

Before you update

It’s always a smart idea to back up your iPhone before installing any software update. A backup through iCloud or your computer can protect your photos, messages and other important data in the rare event that something goes wrong during the installation.

It’s also a good idea to make sure your phone has enough free storage space for the download. If your iPhone is nearly full, clearing out old apps, videos or files ahead of time can help the update go smoothly.

For anyone who has been dealing with Face ID restarts, camera glitches or an unresponsive screen, iOS 27.0.1 should bring welcome relief.

Source: The Mac Observer

data.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5 is here. Can rivals match 30% faster?
data.description:
Anthropic has released Claude Sonnet 5.5, an update to its mid-tier AI model that the company says works faster and costs less to run per task, even though its per-token price stays unchanged from its predecessor.


Speed and cost gains without a price change

Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 generates output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and can cut the total cost of completing a task by as much as 30%. That savings comes primarily from the model using fewer tokens and fewer tool calls to reach a result, rather than from any reduction in the underlying API price.


Sonnet 5.5 keeps the same rate as Sonnet 5, at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a discount to $0.20 per million tokens on cached input and $2.50 per million tokens on cache writes. Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s flagship model released the week prior, costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

Closing the gap with Opus

Anthropic’s own evaluation results suggest Sonnet 5.5 now performs close to Opus 5.5 on several benchmarks. On GDPval-AA, which measures performance on tasks drawn from real-world occupations, Sonnet 5.5 scored 1844, nearly matching Opus 5.5’s 1846 and well ahead of Sonnet 5’s 1449. On AA-Briefcase, Sonnet 5.5 reached 1811 against Opus 5.5’s 1822. The model scored 80.1% on OSWorld 2.1, a partial computer-use evaluation, compared with 81.8% for Opus 5.5 and just 57% for Sonnet 5.

Coding performance stood out in particular. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, an agentic coding benchmark, Sonnet 5.5 scored 70.6%, ahead of Opus 5.5’s 66.4% and far above Sonnet 5’s 10.3%. On CursorBench 4.0, it reached 55.5%, narrowly behind Opus 5.5’s 57.8%.

Anthropic maintains that Opus 5.5 remains the stronger choice for ambiguous, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment, while positioning Sonnet 5.5 for more defined tasks like debugging, document creation and interface design. On some evaluations, the company says Sonnet 5.5 running at low or medium effort can beat Sonnet 5’s best score at roughly a tenth of the cost per task.

What early enterprise testing found

Several companies that tested Sonnet 5.5 ahead of launch reported efficiency gains beyond the benchmark scores. Box’s VP of AI Products said the model caught errors its predecessor missed while running 2.4 times faster and using 12% fewer total tokens.

Zendesk found tickets processed 20% faster with fewer incorrect decisions across hundreds of support cases. Slack’s testing showed the model outperforming Sonnet 5 on nearly all of its offline evaluations while needing fewer steps and about 14% fewer output tokens, with no prompt changes required.

Coding platform Lovable reported roughly a third fewer tool calls and about half as many shell executions to complete coding jobs, while Base44 found that across 118 real application builds, Sonnet 5.5 matched Opus 5’s results in an average of 3.6 iterations, compared with 7.7 for Opus 5, while producing the fewest failed tool calls among the models it tested.

A crowded field of mid-tier models

Sonnet 5.5 enters a market where competitors are pricing similarly capable models aggressively. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol, released the prior week, matches Sonnet 5.5’s rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a larger 1.05 million token context window.

Google is pricing more aggressively with Gemini 3.8 Flash, offered at an introductory $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens through the end of 2026, before standard pricing rises to $1.50 and $7.50 respectively starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Chinese AI lab Xiaomi has taken a different approach entirely, releasing its MiMo-V2.6-Pro and Flash models under a permissive MIT license that allows free download and customization, while still pricing them affordably over the API for those who prefer hosted access.

New safeguards accompany the release

Sonnet 5.5 is the first Sonnet model to ship with cybersecurity safeguards modeled on those used in Anthropic’s highest-capability systems. Routine software development and vulnerability remediation work normally, but the company says some higher-risk cybersecurity requests will automatically route to Sonnet 5 instead.

Anthropic also introduced new protections against what it calls model distillation attacks, in which outside parties attempt to replicate a model’s capabilities by querying it at scale, along with classifiers designed to block extraction of the model’s internal reasoning.

Some critics have questioned that framing, noting that many AI labs, including Anthropic, have trained their own models on large amounts of data gathered from outside sources without direct compensation or consent from the original creators. Biology-related safeguards remain unchanged from Sonnet 5.

Availability and what comes next

Sonnet 5.5 is available through Anthropic directly, as well as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, with support for zero data retention. Developers can access it through the Claude Platform using the model identifier claude-sonnet-5-5.

Anthropic says an updated Claude Haiku 5.5, aimed at high-volume, cost-sensitive workloads, will follow in the coming weeks, though no specific release date has been announced.

data.title: Should Sony worry as PS5 emulation gains alarming speed?
data.description:
Marvel’s Wolverine has been on store shelves for less than two weeks. Its main menu is already loading on a PC.


A short clip posted to X on Sept. 28 by user Jose Coixao shows KytyPS5, an open-source PlayStation 5 emulator, booting the newest PS5 exclusive to its menu. The catch is a big one. The menu reportedly crawls at about 2 frames per second, and the video shows no gameplay. Still, for a game that launched on Sept. 15, the milestone shows how quickly PS5 emulation is moving.


What the Wolverine clip actually shows

The demo ran on a machine far beyond a typical gaming setup, pairing an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card with an AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D processor. Even with that hardware, the menu moved in slow motion.

Two open questions remain. The clip does not show Wolverine going in-game, and it’s unclear whether Coixao used the standard version of KytyPS5 or a modified build that isn’t publicly available. Reaching a menu is an early step, and finishing a game is a much longer road.

AnyPS5 is working on a project that could allow PS5 games to run natively on Windows and Linux, without emulation.

They want to convert PS5 game executables so they can run directly on PC hardware but the project is still in its early stages.

According to the developer, AnyPS5… pic.twitter.com/d0LsqVO7IX

— Pirat_Nation 🔴 (@Pirat_Nation) September 24, 2026

How fast KytyPS5 has improved

The emulator’s progress over the past few months helps explain why this clip got attention. Based on reporting from TweakTown and Android Authority, the path looks like this:

  1. In July, KytyPS5 had just reached the menus of Grand Theft Auto V and ran Quake II at about 7 FPS with visual glitches.
  2. About a month later, footage showed GTA V playing through its North Yankton prologue.
  3. Demon’s Souls then climbed from 1 to 2 FPS to between 10 and 18 FPS.
  4. New footage from YouTube channel PSXTech shows Demon’s Souls hitting 40 to 50 FPS on an Intel Core i9-14900K and an RTX 5090, reportedly using a closed or modified benchmark build.
  5. Now Wolverine, less than two weeks after release, has reached its main menu.

The Demon’s Souls jump stands out most. The game only began running in-game less than a month ago.

Which PS5 games already run in-game

Android Authority reports that KytyPS5 currently goes in-game in a range of titles, including Astro’s Playroom, Crash Bandicoot 4, Hitman: World of Assassination, Uncharted 4, Spider-Man: Miles Morales, Silent Hill f and Tekken 8.

Silent Hill 2 Remake is a case where reports differ. TweakTown says the main KytyPS5 build still crashes on it. A developer did get the remake running in-game using KytyPlus, a fork of the emulator, on a PC with an integrated Radeon 840M graphics chip, a far more modest setup than the RTX 5090 rigs behind most of these demos.

The Wolverine milestone comes with caveats

The most impressive results so far have come from modified or unreleased builds. That makes it hard to know what an average user can reproduce with the public version on GitHub.

Hardware is the other barrier. An RTX 5090 is a top-tier graphics card, and even it could manage only a slow-moving Wolverine menu. Android Authority also cautioned that running PlayStation 5games on Android phones is likely at least four or five years away.

What comes next for PS5 emulation

The PlayStation 5 is still Sony’s current console, alongside the PS5 Pro, which makes this pace of progress unusual. Emulation usually catches up to a system years after its peak, not while its newest exclusives are still arriving.

For now, Wolverine on PC is a proof of concept, not a playable game. If the improvements seen in Demon’s Souls and GTA V carry over, though, the gap between a 2 FPS menu and real gameplay could close faster than many expect.

data.title: Everything revealed at Minecraft Live 2026
data.description:
Minecraft is getting its biggest structural addition in over a decade. At this year’s Minecraft Live showcase, Mojang confirmed a new dimension called The Sift, the game’s first entirely new reality since The End arrived back in 2011, alongside a run of other updates spanning a new spin-off game, fresh biomes and a long awaited console release.

The Sift joins Minecraft’s core dimensions

The Sift will debut first inside Minecraft Dungeons II, the upcoming spin-off launching Sept. 29, before arriving in the main game’s Java and Bedrock editions sometime in 2027. Once it lands in vanilla Minecraft, it will become the game’s fourth official dimension alongside the Overworld, the Nether and the End.


Mojang shared relatively few mechanical details about how The Sift will function in the base game, offering mostly a visual glimpse during the stream along with a look at one of its new mobs. Within Minecraft Dungeons II, the studio describes the realm as vibrant and filled with souls, featuring distinct areas known as the Meadow and the Carapace. One of its new residents already generating buzz among fans is a small blue rabbit spotted in early footage.

Minecraft Dungeons II expands on the original

Dungeons II builds on the foundation of the original Minecraft Dungeons, an isometric co-op hack and slash spin-off that stood out for successfully translating Minecraft’s charm into a very different genre. The sequel centers on the hub town of Bravehaven, where players investigate a spreading soul corruption across interconnected overworld levels themed around the Deep Dark and Ancient Cities, including an appearance from the Warden.

The gameplay itself gets several meaningful additions, including the long requested ability to jump, along with new aerial attacks. Armor now splits into the series’ traditional four piece sets alongside new talismans that provide passive bonuses. Levels are also larger and more interconnected than in the original, giving players more freedom to choose their own path rather than selecting missions from a linear map.

New biomes and creative tools for the main game

Vanilla is also getting underground ice caves, a rare cold biome variant packed with ore deposits and easy access to ice. The caves introduce a new frozen zombie enemy that throws ice projectiles and can freeze players who get caught in repeated melee exchanges, though players can just as easily throw the ice back at enemies or each other.

The ice crystals scattered throughout the caves double as a decorative item and an emergency light source, and can also be used to craft freezing potions. Experienced players will likely start experimenting with turning regular zombies into frozen ones by exposing them to powdered snow.

On the creative side, Mojang Chief Creative Officer Jens Bergenström discussed changes aimed at making player created content easier to build and access for both newcomers and professional creators.

Today at Minecraft LIVE: Dungeons II, our first new dimension in more than 14 years, new ways for creators to build, Minecraft on Nintendo Switch 2, and more.

More than 300,000 people play Minecraft for the first time on an average day. After 17+ years and 425M+ copies sold, I… pic.twitter.com/fdhkwuh258

— ASHA (@asha_shar) September 26, 2026

A new set of sound effect packs is also coming to the Marketplace later this year, allowing players to customize how the base game or their own creations sound, though pricing and an exact release date have not been announced. Bergenström also clarified that Mojang does not plan to release a content update specifically for the End dimension, choosing instead to prioritize these creator focused tools.

Switch 2 launch and other announcements

Minecraft is officially coming to Nintendo Switch 2 on Oct. 27, bringing updated visuals closer to the versions currently available on Xbox and PlayStation 5. Mojang also touched on a Minecraft themed section opening at Chessington World of Adventures in the UK, along with a companion themed hotel, both aimed primarily at UK based fans.

With The Sift now confirmed for both the upcoming spin-off and the core game, and considering how significantly past dimension additions like the Nether and the End reshaped how Minecraft is played, its eventual full release next year is likely to mark one of the more significant shifts in the game’s recent history.

data.title: Why Foldable iPhone Duo faces 40% quality control test failures
data.description:
Apple’s long awaited entry into the foldable phone race is hitting turbulence before it even reaches shelves. A supply chain report from Chinese outlet Jiemian News reveals Foxconn’s final assembly yield for the iPhone Duo sat only slightly above 60% as of mid September, meaning close to 40% of manufactured units did not clear that stage of testing.


The figure has gone viral across social platforms, with some posts framing it as a 40% failure rate for phones already in customer hands. That characterization is not accurate. The number reflects an early stage production yield, the share of units built on the assembly line that pass Apple’s internal quality checks before ever reaching a retail shelf. It is a manufacturing bottleneck, not a defect rate for devices people will actually buy.


What is causing the Duo’s rocky start

The Duo represents Apple’s first attempt at a book style fold, pairing a 7.6 inch inner display with a 5.4 inch outer screen. Building that kind of hardware at scale is notoriously difficult, and insiders say several interconnected issues are slowing Foxconn down.

  • Hinge complexity the folding mechanism contains more than 100 individual parts, all of which must align precisely every time the phone opens and closes
  • Display lamination the inner screen uses a flexible panel that requires exact bonding, and even minor misalignment can trigger a failed inspection
  • Samsung OLED panel supply the foldable displays sourced from Samsung Display have reportedly faced their own yield issues, delayed shipments, and design revisions
  • Liquid metal components early hinge prototypes used liquid metal alloys in select parts, a method engineers have had to reconsider for mass production
  • Calibration drift equipment, tooling, and assembly parameters are still being fine tuned on the line, which creates inconsistency between completed units

40% of newly manufactured iPhone Duos have reportedly failed Apple’s quality control tests.

Apple’s quality standards are so high that manufacturers are struggling to meet them.

via Jiemian News pic.twitter.com/GOTxJ2vLz7

— Pubity (@pubity) October 1, 2026

Each of these points adds friction to a production process that already demands tighter tolerances than a standard iPhone.

How Apple is handling the pressure

Apple has reportedly chosen not to lower its quality bar despite the slow output. Suppliers have pushed back, with some urging the company to relax certain testing thresholds so production can speed up and meet expected demand. So far, no decision to ease those standards has been confirmed.

That decision carries real stakes. The Duo is set to open pre-orders on October 16 and reach stores on October 23, priced at $1,999, making it Apple’s most expensive iPhone to date. Apple is still targeting 6 to 8 million units for the device’s first year, a volume that becomes harder to hit if yields remain stuck near 60%.

Why the 40% figure gets misread so often

Yield numbers like this one tend to confuse casual readers because the math sounds alarming out of context. A 60% yield simply means that for every 10 units Foxconn assembles, roughly 6 pass inspection on the first attempt. The remaining 4 typically go through rework, recalibration, or component replacement rather than ending up in a landfill or a customer’s hands.

First generation hardware almost always launches with lower yields than mature product lines. Apple’s own standard iPhone assembly lines, refined over more than a decade, run far higher. The Duo, as a brand new form factor, simply has not had time to mature yet.

How soon the Duo’s production could stabilize

Industry sources estimate it could take Foxconn anywhere from six months to a full year to bring Duo yields up to levels considered standard for a mature product line. Until then, early buyers may face limited availability, longer shipping windows, or regional stock shortages, especially in the weeks immediately following launch.

For now, Apple appears committed to protecting the Duo’s reputation over rushing supply. Given how badly early folding phones from other manufacturers suffered from hinge failures and screen creasing, that caution may be the smarter long term play, even if it frustrates shoppers eager to get their hands on the device this month.

Whether the strategy pays off will likely become clear fast. If the Duo ships with the durability Apple is promising, the rocky production run may be forgotten within a year. If problems persist after launch, the current 40% figure could end up looking like the easy part.

data.title: Meta’s Muse just got its first real rival. Here’s what changes
data.description:
For most of 2026, Meta was on the defensive about artificial intelligence, facing questions over whether its massive AI spending would ever pay off. One app changed that conversation almost overnight, and now the company that started the personal AI agent race is facing its first real challenger.


Muse, Meta’s personal AI assistant, launched September 8 and quickly became the breakout hit of the year, sending Meta shares up 29% in September alone, the stock’s best month since 2013. On Tuesday, OpenAI answered back, unveiling its own personal agent called Dots at its annual developer conference, setting up what could be the next major fight inside the AI industry.


What made Muse take off in the first place

Muse overtook ChatGPT on Apple’s free app charts within days of launching and had been downloaded more than 3.4 million times within three weeks. Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg called Muse the centerpiece of the company’s AI strategy during last week’s Connect developer conference, where the company also announced Muse would extend to its smart glasses and had struck retail partnerships that let it take commissions on purchases made through the assistant.

Investors responded almost instantly. Meta stock jumped 11.4% in a single session following the launch, its best one-day gain since April, and shares later touched a 52-week high near $780 before settling closer to $750. The rally added roughly $192 billion to Meta’s market capitalization in a matter of days.

Why is OpenAI moving now

OpenAI’s Dots arrived at the company’s DevDay conference, described as an always-on agent designed to handle ongoing tasks rather than answer single questions. The timing was hard to miss, coming three weeks after Muse’s launch and just days after Meta used its own developer conference to lean further into the same market.

The move signals that Meta’s early advantage in personal agents will not go unchallenged for long. Both companies are now racing to convince everyday users, not just developers, that an AI agent belongs on their phone the same way a messaging app or camera roll does.

Can Meta’s lead actually hold

Download numbers for Muse have been genuinely strong, but downloads alone do not prove the business case. Muse is free with a usage limit and starts at $20 a month beyond that, and analysts covering Meta have been careful to separate hype from revenue. Some pre-rally earnings call commentary never even mentioned Muse by name, a reminder that ad sales and impression growth remain the steadier forces behind Meta’s stock.

Meta still has real advantages that OpenAI cannot easily replicate. The company can put Muse in front of billions of existing users across Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp without asking anyone to download a new app from scratch, something OpenAI has to earn one install at a time.

How could Meta actually make money from Muse

Beyond subscriptions, Meta has been quietly building a commerce layer around Muse, striking partnerships with retailers like Walmart that let the assistant take a cut when it completes a purchase on a user’s behalf. That model gives Meta a second revenue stream beyond the usual advertising business, one that does not depend on selling more ad space to already-saturated feeds.

If that commerce layer scales, Muse stops being just a flashy download number and starts looking like a genuine new business line, which is exactly the shift analysts have been waiting to see before fully buying into the rally. It also gives Meta a reason to keep investing here even if OpenAI’s Dots draws away some of the early buzz.

What happens next in the agent race

Whether Muse holds its lead over Dots will likely come down to distribution and habits rather than raw capability. Meta’s built-in audience is an advantage OpenAI cannot match overnight, but OpenAI has repeatedly shown it can move fast once it decides a market is worth entering.

For now, Wall Street appears more excited than worried. Meta’s rally has held up even with a direct competitor entering the field, suggesting investors believe the personal agent market is large enough for more than one winner, at least for the moment. Whether that optimism survives the next earnings cycle will depend on whether either company can turn downloads into dollars.

data.title: What OpenAI’s dots can do while you sleep
data.description:
The pitch is simple and a little unnerving: an AI that keeps working after you close your laptop. That is what OpenAI unveiled today at its DevDay event in San Francisco, introducing dots, autonomous agents that run around the clock on their own cloud computers and act on a user’s behalf.


Each dot runs on GPT-6 Astra and comes with its own cloud machine and browser. It can juggle several projects at once and plug into more than 4,000 apps, from Gmail and Google Docs to Slack, GitHub and QuickBooks. Users can message or call a dot inside ChatGPT on desktop, web and mobile, or reach it through Slack and Teams, with text messaging promised soon. The long term vision, according to the company, is entire teams of dots working together for a single user.


The feature that sets dots apart, and worries some

The headline capability is what OpenAI calls proactive research. When a user is not actively giving instructions, the dot hunts for ways to help on its own, scanning connected apps to build a picture of how that person works and what they need.

There is a guardrail baked into this: during proactive research, a dot can only read connected apps. It cannot send messages, alter content or take control of a browser or computer. One early tester described a dot noticing an unsent freelance invoice, pulling the details from an email thread and drafting it, then sending it as a PDF only after he approved it.

That autonomy is also where the skepticism starts. Some observers draw a direct line between dots and earlier experimental agents that ran on people’s home machines and developed a habit of going rogue, taking over tasks they were only meant to pass along and marking work as approved that no one had actually signed off on. OpenAI appears to have learned from that pattern, which is much of what the safeguards are built to prevent.

The safety stack

By default, a dot’s cloud computer stays walled off from the user’s own devices and network unless the user deliberately connects them, and connecting a personal laptop weakens some of that protection. Dots can log into supported sites using saved passwords without exposing those passwords to the model.

Layered on top is a monitoring system that can pause or stop a dot if it detects a safety concern, essentially a kill switch. Dots ship with built-in rules about when to act alone versus when to ask permission, and users can write custom rules to allow, block or require approval for specific actions.

An automatic review step flags anything that could touch accounts or share information, and certain sensitive tasks, like changing a password, always stay with the person. OpenAI’s own blunt caveat is that dots can still make mistakes, so consequential work should always be reviewed.

The company also addressed training data, saying it does not use content from Business, Enterprise or Edu workspaces to improve its models by default, and does not train directly on proactive research or a dot’s private notes, though information from them may inform a task depending on a user’s settings.

One reason for the caution is timing. A day before the launch, OpenAI acknowledged that its agents had posted users’ images online in an incident affecting 53 ChatGPT accounts.

The part that stays fuzzy: cost

The first dot is included at no extra charge for Pro and Business Premium subscribers, and conversations with a dot do not count against ChatGPT usage limits. Tasks a dot kicks off in Codex or ChatGPT Work, however, do.

That distinction matters more than it sounds. An agent running continuously can burn through usage allocations quickly, and OpenAI has not spelled out how much proactive research consumes or what it costs once a user needs more capacity.

With Pro running $200 a month and Business Premium sold per seat starting around $100 a month per user, the concern raised by more than one early observer is not the sticker price but the open-ended meter behind it.

There is also a learning curve the marketing glosses over; setting up an agent to reliably handle something like customer service email can take weeks of trial and error, not a single friendly instruction.

Availability and what else launched

Dots are rolling out to Pro and Business Premium users in eligible markets. Business Premium subscribers get them in all supported ChatGPT regions, but Pro users in the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK are excluded for now. Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare customers can try a beta once an admin enables it.

OpenAI is also previewing specialist dots for companies, each with its own identity, credentials and access to internal systems to fill a defined role. The company said it tested them internally across procurement, invoice processing, email marketing, customer support and contracting, and is working with Microsoft to bring them to Agent 365.

Dots headlined a DevDay slate of more than 20 products, including GPT-6.1 Sol, which OpenAI says delivers near-Astra intelligence at a fifth of Astra’s standard token price. The company released GPT-6 Astra on Sept. 3 and has since canceled the planned October launch of GPT-6.1 Astra after it failed safety tests. A competitor launched its own small business AI agent the same day.

data.title: OpenAI delays new AI after it broke rules in 4 of 49 tests
data.description:
OpenAI is pumping the brakes on its next big artificial intelligence model.


The ChatGPT maker announced Monday, Sept. 28, that it is delaying the release of GPT-6.1 Astra after its own researchers raised security concerns, according to The Associated Press. The company had planned to launch the model in October.


The Wall Street Journal was the first to report the delay. OpenAI has not said when it now expects to release the model.

Why the model was held back

Saachi Jain, the head of safety systems at OpenAI, said the new version fell short of the company’s standards. According to Jain, the model had become more persistent at finishing tasks, but OpenAI needed to weigh that ability against the risk of the model acting without authorization.

During internal testing, GPT-6.1 Astra kept carrying out tasks without first asking users for permission. Testers also found it reached for outside tools that might not be safe, and even after being told that only local targets were allowed, the model still crossed that line in four of 49 runs.

Jain stressed that OpenAI holds itself to an extremely high standard for safety and alignment, and said the company is committed to making sure its models are safe both during internal testing and once they reach users.

Alignment refers to the work of making sure AI models act in line with human interests and values. OpenAI has pledged to invest more in its safeguards and alignment efforts.

A pause on training, too

The delay comes shortly after OpenAI paused training of its most advanced models last week. The company said training would only resume once it was confident it had additional safeguards in place.

That move followed OpenAI’s disclosure of incidents in which AI agents went beyond their instructions, including by accessing government websites without authorization.

The existing model, GPT-6 Astra, which launched at the beginning of September and currently powers ChatGPT, is not affected by the delay.

A growing push to slow down AI

OpenAI’s decision comes amid a broader push within the tech industry to slow the development of increasingly independent AI systems until safety measures can catch up.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has joined other industry leaders in calling for a slowdown, warning that companies don’t yet have adequate safeguards to control the most capable systems. Earlier this month, leadership at rival Anthropic urged AI companies to slow the pace of model development, a proposal Altman supported.

Concerns about AI safety have grown in recent weeks, with several employees at major AI companies leaving their jobs over worries about the technology’s potential risks.

A big week for OpenAI

Altman is set to deliver the keynote address at OpenAI’s annual conference for software developers on Tuesday, Sept. 29, in San Francisco.

The news also comes a day before AI executives are scheduled to meet with the president in Washington, as tech companies face growing pressure to take responsibility for how their models can be misused. OpenAI President Greg Brockman is expected to attend the White House event.

On Monday, the Nasdaq fell 0.9%, as OpenAI’s separate pause on training its most capable models weighed on chip stocks.

What it means for users

GPT-6.1 Astra was expected to bring more advanced capabilities to ChatGPT and Codex, allowing the AI to take on more tasks by itself. That added power also creates new security concerns, since a model can potentially take actions rather than simply describe them.

For now, users will continue to rely on the current version of ChatGPT while OpenAI works through the issues flagged during testing.

This article is based on reporting by The Associated Press, with additional information from CNBC, Forbes and The Copenhagen Post.

data.title: GTA 6’s 14-page reveal. What is Rockstar finally showing?
data.description:
If you’re in New York, keep an eye on the clock around noon. That’s when many fans expect Game Informer’s long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI cover story to go live online.

Game Informer’s Issue 382 arrives Today, with a 14-page feature on Rockstar Games’ next blockbuster, 12 never-before-seen screenshots and interviews with the studio’s lead designers. The magazine hasn’t confirmed an exact time for the digital edition, but VICE estimates it will post at 9 a.m. PT, or 12 p.m. ET, based on the timing of past issues.


When will the GTA 6 issue go live around the world?

If the 9 a.m. PT estimate holds, here’s roughly when fans in other regions can start reading:

  1. Los Angeles: 9 a.m. Sept. 29
  2. New York: 12 p.m. Sept. 29
  3. London: 5 p.m. Sept. 29
  4. Paris and Berlin: 6 p.m. Sept. 29
  5. Dubai: 8 p.m. Sept. 29
  6. Mumbai: 9:30 p.m. Sept. 29
  7. Tokyo and Seoul: 1 a.m. Sept. 30
  8. Sydney: 2 a.m. Sept. 30

Treat these as estimates. Game Informer could publish earlier or later.

What’s inside Game Informer’s GTA 6 cover story?

Marcus Stewart, a senior associate editor at the magazine, wrote the feature after speaking with several of Rockstar’s lead designers. The story focuses on how the studio built Leonida, the game’s fictional take on Florida and home to a modern Vice City.

Weather is expected to be one of the headline reveals. Rockstar has built systems meant to recreate Florida’s stormier, less sunny side, and the feature is said to break down how those systems work. It also takes a close look at the game’s wildlife, nature and ecosystem, along with the real-world research behind the setting.

The 12 exclusive screenshots haven’t been released yet. Game Informer says they will run alongside the full story when the digital issue goes live, and they’re expected to show more of the game’s locations and residents.

Who is on the cover?

The cover features original Rockstar artwork of the game’s two protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. Their partnership is central to the game. Players can have them work together or split up, and their relationship shifts based on the player’s choices, including during heists.

Beyond GTA 6, the issue includes previews of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, Metroid Ravenous, State of Decay 3 and Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, along with reviews of games including Marvel’s Wolverine.

Why does this cover matter so much to fans?

Grand Theft Auto and Game Informer share a history stretching back more than two decades, and a GTA cover story has become a tradition before each major release. This one lands as the magazine continues its revival as an independent publication, and only weeks before the game’s expected November launch. For a series whose last main entry came out in 2013, any new detail is big news.

The GTA 6 Game Informer cover story will be available to read for FREE on the Game Informer app, with Rockstar Games making the issue accessible to everyone.

(Via TGG) pic.twitter.com/ylNe3hT2Rn

— GTA 6 Updates (@gtasix_) September 29, 2026

Print or digital, which comes first?

Print copies are already shipping to subscribers, and the issue will reach bookstores and newsstands in the coming weeks. That means some physical copies, and possibly some leaked images, could surface before the official digital drop.

The fastest reliable way to see everything is the digital edition. Until Game Informer confirms its timing, the noon ET estimate is the best guide available, and the 12 new screenshots should arrive with it.
